query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys processed under identical rapid solidification conditions, the nature of the element X (Al, Mn, or Si) governs the formation and persistence of a protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C. Specifically, the high oxygen affinity of Al drives the formation of a slow-growing, coherent, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale that acts as a diffusion barrier, whereas Mn- and Si-bearing alloys form oxides with higher defect densities and thermal expansion mismatches, leading to rapid, unstable oxidation with cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase metallic solid-solution CrFeCoNiX (with X = Al, Mn, or Si) produced via rapid solidification under identical conditions.
generation.intervention: Prepare three compositional variants by melting and rapid solidification to ensure a single-phase state, ensuring identical processing conditions for alloys with X = Al, Mn, and Si.
generation.conditions: Expose polished samples to a controlled oxidative (or corrosive) atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C (e.g., 100 hours of continuous exposure) in a laboratory furnace.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and continuity of the surface oxide film—specifically, the formation of a continuous, dense alumina layer in Al-bearing alloys versus discontinuous, defective oxide films in Mn- or Si-bearing alloys.
generation.mechanism: The mechanistic basis is that Al’s high oxygen affinity encourages the formation of a stoichiometric, low-defect, slow-growing alumina scale that can act as an effective diffusion barrier. In contrast, when X is Mn or Si, the oxides that form have higher defect densities and exhibit thermal expansion mismatches with the substrate, resulting in localized stresses that cause cracking or spallation of the oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: After exposure above 900 °C, Al-bearing CrFeCoNiX alloys will display a uniform, adherent, and stable protective alumina scale, whereas the Mn- and Si-bearing alloys will develop oxide scales that are discontinuous, cracked, or prone to spallation. Falsification occurs if Mn- or Si-bearing alloys also form stable, coherent oxide layers comparable to the Al variant.
generation.baseline: All alloys are processed by the same rapid solidification route to ensure a single-phase state and are exposed under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions, so that differences in oxide behavior can be attributed solely to the effect of the element X.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single-phase solid-solution state exposed to sustained high-temperature conditions (>900 °C) in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. Behavior in multiphase alloys or under thermal cycling conditions may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative differences in oxide formation are expected based on elemental oxygen affinities and known diffusion behavior, the quantitative aspects such as exact oxide growth rates, the threshold levels of defect density leading to spallation, and long-term stability under cyclic conditions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate three sets of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples (with X = Al, Mn, or Si) using identical rapid solidification methods to ensure a single-phase state. Polish the samples and subject them to a high-temperature oxidative exposure at >900 °C for 100 hours in a controlled furnace. Post-exposure, perform comprehensive surface analyses.
measurements: SEM and TEM imaging to assess the continuity and adhesion of the oxide scales
XRD analysis to determine the oxide phases and crystallographic coherency
EDS mapping to evaluate elemental distribution across the oxide–substrate interface
Mechanical adhesion tests to quantify the bond strength of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn- or Si-bearing alloys exhibit oxide scales that are continuous, adherent, and show similar phase purity and diffusional blockage properties as the Al-bearing alloys, then the hypothesis that element X's nature governs the stability and coherence of the protective oxide is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. The high rate of heating and cooling and high oxygen concentration during spraying led to oxidation development prior to decomposition of the supersaturated solid solution. Depleted Al layers of BCC transferred to the FCC phase. cited_evidence.text: Thus, during prolonged isothermal annealing, the decomposition of the supersaturated BCC solid solution with sigma phase formation occurs earlier than oxidation. The phase transformation sequence in FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 particles during HVOF deposition and annealing in air atmosphere is different. High temperature and high oxygen concentration in spraying lead to oxidation development prior to supersaturated solid solution decomposition. Due to the extremely high rate of heating and cooling during HVOF spraying, the sigma phase has no sufficient time to form. Zones of supersaturated BCC solid solution that are depleted in Al transfer to FCC. In contrast, under annealing, the supersaturated BCC solid solution decomposition occurs earlier than pronounced oxidation, observable with XRD. The decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation occurs in the temperature interval of 600–800 °C, and over 800 °C the pronounced oxidation with alumina formation begins. Alumina growth leads to the appearance of FCC in the zones depleted in Al. During prolonged annealing at 800 °C, the subsurface layer is enriched with Cr, Fe, and Mo, which prevent FCC formation.

Data for parabolic rate constants of various oxides demonstrates the superiority of Al2O3 and SiO2 scales over other oxides []. Al2O3 and SiO2 are highly stable and exhibit low diffusivities for cations and anions. Al2O3 has small deviations from stoichiometry, low point defect concentrations, and high melting point (2050 °C). SiO2 is more permeable to oxygen and nitrogen than alumina at high temperature and has a lower melting temperature []. The activation energy for diffusion of oxygen in silica is lower than in alumina. Thus, alumina becomes less effective oxidation barrier than silica as temperature is increased. Nevertheless, Al2O3 is an excellent barrier to penetration by oxygen and grows at a slower rate than silica at temperatures to about 1300 °C. Alumina and/or SiO2 scales would be desirable to form on Nb-silicide based alloys. The activity of Al required for the formation of Al2O3 cannot be provided by the Al concentration in the Nb-silicide based alloys owing to the effect of the latter on mechanical behaviour at low and high temperatures. Formation of SiO2 is more likely but depends on alloy microstructure and the formation of Nb2O5 on the scale (see below).

proposals.material_system: CrFeCoNiX HEAs where X = Al versus X = Mn or Si in a single-phase metallic solid-solution state
proposals.intervention: Prepare three compositional variants by alloying with Al, Mn, or Si under identical melting and rapid solidification (single‐phase) conditions
proposals.conditions: Expose polished samples to a controlled oxidative (or corrosive) atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for a prolonged period (e.g., 100 hours) in a lab furnace
proposals.structural_mediator: The formation (or absence) of a continuous, dense oxide film—principally Al2O3 in the Al-bearing alloy versus less protective Mn- or Si-oxides
proposals.mechanism: High oxygen affinity of Al promotes formation of a slow-growing, coherent alumina layer that acts as a diffusion barrier; in contrast, Mn or Si yield oxides with higher defect density and thermal expansion mismatch, leading to cracking/spallation
proposals.predicted_outcome: Only the Al-alloy will develop and sustain a stable, adherent protective oxide layer at >900 °C, while Mn- and Si-alloys develop unstable, cracked/spalled oxide scales; a controlled baseline is provided by comparing identical processing and exposures across variants
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It directly tests the hypothesis that the element X governs the oxidation behaviour through its affinity for oxygen and oxide film properties, with a clear comparative baseline and falsification criterion (if even Mn/Si systems form a protective layer, the hypothesis would be refuted)

proposals.material_system: CrFeCoNiX HEAs (X = Al, Mn or Si) in single-phase versus multiphase states
proposals.intervention: Produce two sets of each alloy by varying post-casting thermal treatments: a rapid quench to retain a homogeneous single-phase structure and a slow cooling/annealing regime to induce multiphase segregation
proposals.conditions: Expose both sets to an oxidative and/or corrosive environment at temperatures above 900 °C for durations on the order of tens of hours
proposals.structural_mediator: The microstructural homogeneity (absence of interphase boundaries) in the single-phase version versus the presence of phase boundaries or intermetallic precipitates in the multiphase state
proposals.mechanism: In the single-phase state, uniform elemental distribution promotes coherent oxide layer formation (e.g., continuous Al2O3 in the Al case), whereas in the multiphase state, chemical heterogeneity and divergent oxidation kinetics at phase boundaries induce localized stresses, leading to oxide cracking and spallation
proposals.predicted_outcome: Only the single-phase HEA variant will demonstrate a persistent and coherent protective oxide, while the multiphase variant will show unstable oxide formation; falsification would occur if both processing routes lead to similar oxidation stability
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It assesses whether microstructural state (single- vs multiphase) governs the stability and coherency of oxide scales at high temperature, with a controlled comparison for a given overall composition

proposals.material_system: CrFeCoNiAl high-entropy alloy processed via different synthesis routes
proposals.intervention: Fabricate samples via high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying and by conventional casting, ensuring the same nominal composition but different initial oxide precursors and microstructures
proposals.conditions: Maintain post-processing exposures in an oxidative atmosphere at >900 °C for an extended period (e.g., 50–100 hours) to evaluate high-temperature scale evolution
proposals.structural_mediator: The pre-formed thin oxide scale (or depletion layer) that originates during rapid thermal cycling in HVOF, versus the as-cast state lacking such pre-oxidation features
proposals.mechanism: The HVOF route produces a built-in, adherent, Al-depleted surface layer that acts as a template for forming a coherent, protective alumina scale upon further high-temperature exposure, whereas the cast material, with a more typical, defect-laden oxide, develops unstable scales
proposals.predicted_outcome: HVOF-processed HEA samples will display a more uniform, stable, and coherent protective oxide after exposure compared to the cast samples; falsification occurs if both exhibit similar oxidation behavior
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It isolates the effect of processing-induced pre-oxidation features on subsequent oxide stability, thus testing whether initial surface conditions govern the long-term persistence of the protective oxide layer

proposals.material_system: CrFeCoNiX HEAs (emphasizing the Mn-bearing variant) analyzed via thermodynamic modeling and in situ high-temperature characterization
proposals.intervention: Integrate CALPHAD-based thermodynamic simulations with in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) studies during oxidation at 900–1100 °C
proposals.conditions: Perform experiments in a precisely controlled oxidative/corrosive atmosphere with real-time phase monitoring during heating cycles above 900 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: The phase evolution and oxide formation kinetics as captured by real-time diffraction peaks and lattice strain measurements
proposals.mechanism: Element-specific oxygen affinities (and the resultant differences in kinetic diffusion rates) determine whether oxide layer growth is self-limiting and coherent (e.g., formation of a protective spinel or Cr/Mn oxide) or rapid and volatile, leading to cracking; the model correlates predicted oxide phases with their mechanical integrity
proposals.predicted_outcome: In situ HTXRD will reveal that alloys with a specific element (depending on X) have a gradual, coherent oxide scale formation evidenced by stable, low-strain diffraction features, while a rapid, disordered oxide phase with transient features indicates a tendency to spall; a falsifying observation would be a mismatch between the predicted and observed oxide sequences or kinetics
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By marrying thermodynamic predictions with real-time experimental evidence, this approach tests the mechanistic hypothesis that elemental diffusion, oxidation rates, and phase evolution govern the persistence of a protective oxide vs unstable spalling, thus fulfilling the requirement for a testable, single-mechanism hypothesis

decision.rationale: Direction D directly addresses the central question by comparing CrFeCoNiX alloys where X is Al versus Mn or Si under identical single‐phase processing and high-temperature oxidation conditions. The hypothesis in this direction posits that the intrinsic oxygen affinity of the X element governs the nature of the oxide scale: Al promotes a slow‐growing, coherent alumina layer that serves as a protective diffusion barrier, whereas Mn and Si yield oxides with higher defect density and thermal expansion mismatches that are prone to cracking and spallation. This comparison against a defined baseline of identical processing routes and exposures is straightforward, testable, and well supported by prior evidence on the oxidation behavior of alumina versus non‐alumina oxides.
